title: By whose grace, the body
hook: by His grace you have a healthy body and a home

segments.voice: Yesterday, by whose grace: the drumbeat over dinner and a good shirt. Your line was by his grace, this meal. Did you remember it at a meal? Today the same two words come closer to home. Day four hundred sixty.

Most of us only notice our bodies when something goes wrong. A sprained ankle, and suddenly every step is a project. A cold, and you'd give anything for one clear breath through the nose. Then it heals, and within a week you've forgotten again. The same with home: you notice the roof the night it leaks. Ashtpadi six keeps repeating jih prasaad, by whose grace, and in its later stanzas it turns from the plate and the wardrobe to the two things we forget most completely: the body we live in, and the house that holds it.
screen: `NOTICED ONLY WHEN IT HURTS.` → `THE ROOF, THE NIGHT IT LEAKS.` → `BY WHOSE GRACE: BODY AND HOME.`

segments.voice: One line says: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee. By whose grace you have a healthy, golden body. Aarog is health, being free of illness. Kanchan is gold. Dehee is the body. A golden body isn't about looks. In the old poetry, gold is what's precious and doesn't tarnish. So: by whose grace this precious, working body is yours. The second half, as always, turns: attune yourself to that loving Lord. And the same ashtpadi has already spoken of the house: by whose grace you live in a mansion of comfort, by whose grace you dwell at peace with your family. Another line even says, by whose grace your honor is kept covered, the things you'd rather nobody saw, quietly protected. Put those together and you get a picture of an ordinary good day: you woke up, you could move, nobody embarrassed you, there was a door to close behind you and people inside it. The stanza says none of that is automatic. Each is a jih prasaad. This doesn't mean anyone who is ill, or without a home, has lost grace. Gurbani speaks of rich and poor, healthy and sick, as living within the same hukam, and Sikhs are asked to share what they have, which is why the langar, the gurdwara kitchen, serves a free meal to anyone who comes in. The stanza is speaking to the one who has these things and forgets them, and it asks that person to notice.
screen: `AAROG: HEALTH. KANCHAN: GOLD.` · `DEHEE: THE BODY.` · `A HOUSE, A FAMILY, HONOR KEPT.` · `NOT AUTOMATIC: EACH A GIFT.` · then, large: `BY HIS GRACE, THIS HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank your body and your home. Sit still. Start at your feet: they carried you today. Your hands: they held things. Your lungs: breathing, all by themselves. Whatever hurts, let it be there too; you're not pretending. Then widen out to the room around you, the walls, the roof, whoever shares this home with you, or the quiet if no one does. If you pray, you can give thanks with the words jih prasaad. If you don't, let each part simply be noticed and valued. The bell holds the time.
By whose grace. Today, jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee: by whose grace a healthy, precious body, and a home to live in.
Your line: by his grace, this home. When you walk through your front door today, touch the frame, and say the line once. Day four hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'jih prasaad' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as reminders that health, home and family are gifts, and many share what they have through langar and seva.

fork.setup: your sprained ankle has healed. a week later, by ashtpadi six, what's the move?
options: notice the healthy body as a gift, by whose grace.
fork.reveal: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee: by whose grace this healthy, precious body, and the stanza turns you toward the Giver.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dehee, the body; in ashtpadi six, the 'golden body' given by grace.

trapdoor: what you thought: thanking God for health is a private feeling.
what it means: the stanza ties body, home and family to one Giver, and Sikhs share them in langar and seva.
what a scholar hears: 'aarog kanchan dehee' pairs Sanskrit-derived aarogya (health) with kanchan (gold), a stock image for what is precious and pure.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
